summary: Examines the overhead of moving user data through the end-system network path at high speeds, which has limited the use of Internet protocols in demanding settings. It addresses an IP-based copy avoidance solution through Remote Direct Memory Access. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Copying data again and again slows a fast computer down, like rewriting a letter several times before mailing it. This memo asks how to skip the extra copies.

questions: why is network data copying slow
why is data copying slow on fast networks
what is rdma over ip problem
subtitle: Why copying data wastes CPU and memory bandwidth on fast networks.

tldr.problem: High-speed networks (Gigabit and above) move data faster than memory buses can keep up. Traditional TCP/IP requires copying data multiple times (from network interface to kernel to application), consuming precious memory bandwidth and limiting throughput.
tldr.mechanism: Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) allows the network adapter to place data directly into application buffers without intermediate copies, and lets applications access remote memory directly. This approach has proven robust and scalable in research and commercial deployments.
tldr.outcome: By eliminating copies, systems can achieve much higher throughput (up to 160% improvement in some cases) and leave more CPU available for application processing. RDMA is widely used in databases, storage systems, and high-performance computing on special-purpose networks, and this RFC advocates for IP-based RDMA solutions.

facts.label: Typical copies on receive
facts.value: 2 (network interface to kernel, kernel to application)

today: RFC 4297 is an Informational document and remains the most comprehensive statement of the RDMA over IP problem. RDMA solutions have been standardized in protocols like iWARP (RDMA over TCP), RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet), and others, and are widely deployed in data centers and high-performance computing environments.

sections.title: The High Cost of Data Movement
sections.content:
Network I/O processing in modern systems involves significant overhead from data movement operations—specifically, copying data. On the receive side, data typically makes at least two copies: once from the network interface to kernel buffers, and again from kernel buffers to application buffers. Each copy crosses the memory bus twice, consuming precious memory bandwidth.

Research shows that 48% to 64% of TCP processing overhead is attributable to data touching operations, with copying being the dominant cost. In carefully implemented systems, even after optimizing other factors like checksums, data movement still accounts for a substantial fraction of total processing costs. For messages larger than 128 bytes, data-touching operations dominate the processing costs.

This is not just an academic concern. High-speed refers to conditions where network bandwidth is large compared to CPU and memory bandwidth. Today, this occurs at 1 Gigabit per second and higher speeds. At 10 Gigabit speeds, the problem becomes severe. For example, a 1.2 GHz Athlon processor with 1 GByte/second of memory bandwidth could theoretically handle about 2.67 Gigabits per second of network traffic if 100% of resources were dedicated to copying (which is not possible). A typical modern server with two 1 Gigabit connections cannot keep up.
sections.eli5: When data arrives from the network, a slow computer can handle the copies without trouble. But a fast computer is like a postal worker trying to sort mail by rewriting every address three times—the rewriting becomes the bottleneck, not the delivery.

sections.title: Memory Bandwidth is the Root Cause
sections.content:
The fundamental issue is that memory bandwidth is scarce relative to network bandwidth and CPU bandwidth. This gap has been widening for decades. Microprocessor performance has grown at about 60% per year, while DRAM access time improvements are only 10% per year. The STREAM Benchmark shows processing performance growing at 50% per year from 1985-2001, while sustainable memory bandwidth grows at only 35% per year.

Meanwhile, network bandwidth doubles roughly every 3-4 years. As links increase from 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps and beyond, the problem becomes more acute. A faster CPU does not help if the CPU spends most of its time waiting for memory. The only solution is to reduce the number of times data crosses the memory bus.

This gap particularly affects large systems (multiprocessor machines and clusters) that handle aggregate bandwidths exceeding 1 Gigabit per second. Servers doing transaction processing, e-commerce, web serving, content distribution, video distribution, and backups all suffer from copy overhead. When a significant portion of machine resources are consumed in network I/O rather than application processing, it becomes difficult for the application to scale.
sections.eli5: Computers get faster at computing, but not faster at moving data to where computers can access it. So the memory bus becomes the bottleneck. As networks get faster, this gap gets worse.

sections.title: Affected Applications and Use Cases
sections.content:
The applications most affected by copying overhead are those that manage and distribute Internet and enterprise data. These include database applications for transaction processing (OLTP), e-commerce servers, web serving, decision support systems, content distribution networks, video distribution, and backup systems. These applications are typically run in data centers organized into three tiers: web servers, application servers, and backend databases.

When network I/O consumes too much memory bandwidth, performance on network paths between tiers suffers. The high overhead from network-related memory copies diverts system resources from application processing and creates bottlenecks that limit system throughput. For example, an e-commerce server communicates with both a customer site and a database server; an OLTP server connects to a database and customers; a content distribution server connects to a server farm.

Scaling clustered or multiprocessor systems requires proportional scaling of interconnect bandwidth. Interconnect latency can also limit performance of applications that frequently share data between processors. Excessive network I/O overheads require the use of more processors than optimal and reduce the benefit of adding additional CPUs. Copy avoidance can remove 67% to 80% of the bus bandwidth load, enabling machines to achieve full network bandwidth while leaving CPU cycles available for application work.
sections.eli5: Databases, web servers, and video streaming services all need to move lots of data fast. If copying takes all the CPU time, they cannot handle enough clients or move enough data. Fixing the copying problem makes them work much better.

sections.title: Copy Avoidance Techniques
sections.content:
Research and industry have explored two main approaches to reducing data movement overhead. First, single-host approaches use hardware or software changes within one computer to reduce copying costs. Second, memory-to-memory approaches exchange explicit data placement information between hosts, allowing the network adapter to steer data directly into application buffers, reducing movement.

Software-only approaches have proven problematic. While zero-copy transmit is achievable, zero-copy receive is difficult without strict alignment and no-touch requirements that greatly reduce portability. Optimizations are highly interdependent with system architecture and file system design, making them fragile and difficult to maintain. For example, the Solaris Zero-Copy TCP work, which relied on page remapping, required architecture-specific optimizations that could not be reused across different machines.

In contrast, memory-to-memory systems using RDMA have proven robust, provide good performance, and can be implemented relatively simply. Once implemented, RDMA can be used with any OS and machine architecture without revision when either changes. Examples include Virtual Interface Architecture (VI), Myrinet, Quadrics, InfiniBand, and Fibre Channel. These systems have been widely deployed in scientific computing, data centers for storage and transaction processing, and other high-performance applications.
sections.eli5: You can try to tweak the CPU or the operating system to copy faster, but that is hard and breaks when you upgrade. Or you can tell the network adapter to skip the copies entirely and put data where it belongs. The second approach works much better.

sections.title: Direct Data Placement and RDMA as the Solution
sections.content:
The RDMA solution can be viewed as two distinct components. The first is Direct Data Placement (DDP): the means by which memory is exposed to the remote peer and the means by which the peer may read and write it. DDP allows a sender to attach placement information to data, telling the receiver's network interface exactly where to store it.

The second component is RDMA semantics—control functions layered on top of DDP, including connection management, operation ordering, signaling completions, and a Send facility optimized for hardware implementation. While historically both aspects have been called RDMA, it is useful to distinguish DDP (the data placement facility) from RDMA (the control and management aspect).

By exporting direct memory access across the network, applications can direct the network stack to manage all data directly from application buffers without intermediate copies. This approach scales a machine upwards by removing at least 67% to 80% of the bus bandwidth load, removes bottlenecks from the network processing path, and increases throughput. On machines with limited bus bandwidth, this allows the host to attain full network bandwidth. On machines with adequate bandwidth, it frees CPU cycles for application processing, sometimes dramatically improving system capacity.
sections.eli5: The idea is to split the job into two parts: one part tells the network adapter where to put data (DDP), and another part provides all the control and safety checks (RDMA). Together they let you send data without any copies and let programs reach across the network and grab what they need.

sections.title: Security Concerns for RDMA Solutions
sections.content:
Solutions that reduce copying overhead may introduce new security concerns. RDMA's direct memory access capability means that a remote peer can read or write local memory with authorization. Any RDMA solution must ensure strong authentication, integrity checking, and authorization controls.

IPsec is identified as a natural fit for securing RDMA placement. Because RDMA avoids buffering, security protection should be performed before transport and RDMA layers process each segment. TLS, which is layered on top of transports and requires buffering entire records before processing, introduces overhead that RDMA is designed to eliminate and is therefore less suitable.

The fundamental challenge is that properties like confidentiality, integrity, and authentication cannot defend against all attacks from properly authenticated peers that might be malicious, compromised, or buggy. Therefore, RDMA design must address protection against such peers. Memory regions must be protected by explicit application control. Peer connections must pass authentication and authorization before beginning RDMA operations. All peer accesses to memory regions must be authenticated and authorized in the context of the connection and endpoint, prior to any data transfer.
sections.eli5: Letting someone reach into your memory is powerful but dangerous. You need strong locks and keys, careful checks that the person is who they say they are, and the ability to say 'you can read but not write' and make the computer enforce it.
